findings.summary: Every page title lags its content by roughly half a page, so each page is filed under the topic it finishes rather than the one it teaches.
findings.evidence: Page 2 is titled "Why HTTP/1.1 Ran Out of Road (cont.)" but after one recap diagram it opens the entire binary-framing chapter: "Frames, Not Lines" / "Smallest unit is a binary frame, not a line of ASCII" / the 9-byte frame header / the frame-type table. The same shift repeats: page 4 "Multiplexing: Many Streams, One Connection" carries "One Queue, Everything Waits" and the three HOL layers; page 5 "Head-of-Line Blocking: Three Layers" carries "Why Not Just gzip" and all of HPACK's tables; page 6 "HPACK: Header Compression in HTTP/2" carries "Push, And Why It Died".
findings.fix: Re-split the page boundaries so each page starts at its own chapter: end page 1 at the SPDY sidebox + mental-model diagram, start page 2 at "Frames, Not Lines" titled "HTTP/2 Binary Framing Layer", start the multiplexing page at "Interleaved Frames", the HOL page at "One Queue, Everything Waits", the HPACK page at "Why Not Just gzip", the push page at "Push, And Why It Died", and the QUIC page at "A Transport, Not A Protocol Version".

findings.summary: The caption advertises "10 pages" but the carousel has only 9 titled pages.
findings.evidence: Caption: "10 pages of study notes on binary framing, HPACK vs QPACK, ..." vs. 9 titles: "Why HTTP/1.1 Ran Out of Road" ... "QUIC: A New Transport on UDP".
findings.fix: Change "10 pages" to "9 pages" in the caption, or add the missing tenth page (an HTTP/3 + QPACK page would also make good on the caption's "HPACK vs QPACK" promise, which no current title covers).

findings.summary: The claim that QUIC connection migration preserves congestion state is wrong — RFC 9000 requires resetting the congestion controller and RTT estimator on the new path.
findings.evidence: "Wi-Fi to cellular keeps the same connection and its congestion state" (bullet under "Connection IDs And Migration")
findings.fix: Change to "Wi-Fi to cellular keeps the same connection, keys and stream state — no re-handshake" and add a note: RFC 9000 §9.4 requires an endpoint to reset the congestion controller and RTT estimator to initial values for the new path (the only exception is a port-only change from NAT rebinding).

findings.summary: QPACK is named as a working part of HTTP/3 but is never defined anywhere in the handbook, which stops mid-chapter.
findings.evidence: Page 9: "One control stream per side, plus QPACK encoder and decoder streams" — the only occurrence of QPACK in the slides. Nothing explains what QPACK is, why HPACK cannot be reused over QUIC, or what the encoder/decoder streams carry. The earlier setup is also left dangling: page 5 says "HPACK's shared dynamic table forces ordered header processing" with no payoff. The caption still promises "HPACK vs QPACK" and "10 pages of study notes" for 9 pages.
findings.fix: Add the QPACK material before the deck ends: HPACK's ordered-delivery assumption breaking under QUIC, QPACK (RFC 9204) static table of 99 entries plus dynamic table with updates on separate unidirectional streams, Required Insert Count and SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS as the compression-vs-independence knob — then correct the caption's page count.

findings.summary: The caption claims 10 pages but the deck has 9 slides.
findings.evidence: caption: "10 pages of study notes on binary framing, HPACK vs QPACK..."; the slides array contains 9 entries (ending at "QUIC: A New Transport on UDP")
findings.fix: Change "10 pages" to "9 pages", or add the missing page.

findings.summary: The caption promises an HPACK vs QPACK comparison that the deck never delivers.
findings.evidence: caption: "HPACK vs QPACK" — QPACK appears exactly once in the body, as "plus QPACK encoder and decoder streams", with no explanation of what it is or how it differs from HPACK
findings.fix: Either drop "vs QPACK" from the caption, or add a short QPACK block (why HPACK's ordered dynamic table breaks over out-of-order QUIC streams; encoder/decoder streams; blocked-streams / insert-count trade-off).

findings.summary: Page 1 content overruns the bottom margin so the "Where h2 Came From" callout's bottom border and the footer ornament are clipped by the page edge.
findings.evidence: Last callout line "· Became HTTP/2: RFC 7540 (2015), revised RFC 9113" sits at roughly y=1380 of a 1440px page; the footer ornament "· · · ✦ · · ·" — fully visible at ~y=1280 on pages 2-9 — is reduced on page 1 to a partial mark touching the bottom edge.
findings.fix: Move the "Where h2 Came From" callout (or the "Latency, Not Bandwidth" callout above it) to the start of page 2 so page 1's last block closes above the footer band.

findings.summary: "Immune" to length-ambiguity smuggling is too strong: HTTP/2 front ends that downgrade to HTTP/1.1 are a well-known smuggling vector.
findings.evidence: "Parsers get simpler and immune to length-ambiguity smuggling"
findings.fix: Change to "length is explicit per frame, so the Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding ambiguity disappears within h2 itself — smuggling returns only when a front end re-serializes h2 to HTTP/1.1 (h2.CL / h2.TE)."

findings.summary: The "The Four Nouns" flowchart renders its leaf nodes in the wrong rows, so the Connection > Streams > Messages > Frames hierarchy does not read as a diagram.
findings.evidence: post.json:238-244 specifies rows ["c0_0","c0_1"] (Messages, Frames side by side) then ["c1_0"] (all streams share it); the render stacks "Messages" above "Frames" in one column and places "all streams share it" beside "Messages", unboxed, while "Connection", "Streams" and "one TCP socket" are boxed.
findings.fix: Fix the flowchart renderer's row layout so each spec row lays out horizontally and leaf nodes get the same box treatment as parent nodes; if a 4-row chart cannot lay out in this column width, replace the diagram with the plain line "Connection > Streams > Messages > Frames" already present in the adjacent bullet.

findings.summary: The stream lifecycle diagram closes page 2 with no caption, and its only explanation sits on page 3 behind unrelated preface material.
findings.evidence: Page 2's last block is a bare flow diagram: {"nodes":["idle","open","half-closed","closed"]}, with no heading or text. Page 3 opens with "Preface And Negotiation" and the `PRI * HTTP/2.0` code block, and only then says "`END_STREAM` flag moves a peer to half-closed".
findings.fix: Add a "Stream Lifecycle" heading above the diagram on page 2 and move the `END_STREAM` bullet up to sit directly under it, leaving page 3 to start cleanly at the connection preface.

findings.summary: The absolute claim that h2 with HTTP/1.1 hacks intact gives zero speedup overstates the effect.
findings.evidence: "Migration rule: enabling h2 without removing hacks yields no speedup"
findings.fix: Change to "enabling h2 without removing the hacks forfeits most of the win" — header compression and the single warm connection still help even with sharding and bundles in place.

findings.summary: The "Undo The Old Hacks" table contains a row whose first column is empty, so "defeats coalescing and HPACK" renders as an orphan row with no label.
findings.evidence: post.json:455-458 defines the row as ["", "defeats coalescing and HPACK"]; the render shows a bordered table row with a blank "h1.1 hack" cell under "Domain sharding".
findings.fix: Merge it into the preceding row as "Domain sharding | splits the shared connection; defeats coalescing and HPACK" so the table has no empty label cell.

findings.summary: HPACK is cited by name as a reason to drop domain sharding one page before header compression is introduced.
findings.evidence: Page 4 table row: ["", "defeats coalescing and HPACK"]. HPACK is first defined on page 5: "HPACK (RFC 7541) is purpose-built instead".
findings.fix: Change the cell to "defeats coalescing and header compression" (the syllabus wording), and keep the HPACK name for page 5 where the compressor is introduced.

findings.summary: The static-table example uses pseudo-header syntax a page before pseudo-headers are explained.
findings.evidence: Page 5 table rows ["2","`:method`","`GET`"], ["4","`:path`","`/`"], ["8","`:status`","`200`"] appear with no account of the leading colon; page 6 first explains it: "`:method: GET`      # pseudo-headers come first" and "`:status` for responses".
findings.fix: Move the pseudo-header bullets (`:method`/`:scheme`/`:authority`/`:path`, `:status`, must precede regular headers) ahead of the static-table rows, or add one line before the table stating that HTTP/2 replaces the request line and status line with colon-prefixed pseudo-headers.

findings.summary: Saying RFC 9114 "omits push" is false and contradicts the deck's own HTTP/3 frame table.
findings.evidence: "HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) omits push in practice; the ecosystem moved on" — yet page 9's table lists "push cap | `SETTINGS` | `MAX_PUSH_ID`"
findings.fix: Reword to: "HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) still specifies push — `PUSH_PROMISE`, `MAX_PUSH_ID`, `CANCEL_PUSH` — but no major browser implements it."
